missed: The training should cover the goals of § 38(3) BSIG: recognising and assessing risks and risk management, and judging what they mean for your company's services.

We offer a course for this on this platform. You can also choose any other provider; the law does not require providers to be accredited.

learn.title: Who works for your company
body: The security of your IT also covers whoever works on it from outside or can reach your data: service providers, software vendors, suppliers. The law calls them your direct suppliers and service providers. The first step is a list of who they are and what they do for you.
Start with the ones your business could not run without. The list grows over time.
learn.duty: The law requires measures for supply chain security, including in your relationships with your direct suppliers and service providers.

5_2.headline: Record what you have agreed with your suppliers
5_2.teaser: For each supplier: what does the contract say about security?
missed: If a service provider processes personal data on your behalf, part of this is already settled in the data processing agreement: it must take the measures of Art. 32 GDPR and notify you of personal data breaches without undue delay (Art. 28(3)(c) and Art. 33(2) GDPR). A security incident that does not involve personal data is not covered.
Large providers rarely negotiate. Then what counts is their standard terms. Read them before you choose "None of this is agreed".

learn.title: What is agreed with each one
body: Your suppliers are on the list, and you have rated the risk at each one. Now it is about the relationship itself: what is agreed with each of them so that they work securely for you?

When you choose the measures, the law asks you to take into account each supplier's vulnerabilities and the quality of its products and security practice. Contracts are the usual place: in Germany, the explanatory memorandum names contracts on security measures, incident handling and updates as examples. They are one way, not the only one; you can also, for example, limit a service provider's access.
learn.duty: The law requires supply chain security, including the security aspects of your relationships with your direct suppliers and service providers.

rows.name: Incidents
rows.detail: It tells us without undue delay of every security incident that may affect our systems or data, and helps us deal with it.

rows.name: Updates
rows.detail: It installs security updates for the systems it looks after promptly and tells us when a system no longer receives updates.

clause.note: In Germany, the legislator names these three topics as examples (explanatory memorandum to § 30 BSIG, Bundestag printed paper 21/1501, p. 148). The law prescribes no particular wording.

If your portal also records a contact person, add updating it to what happens when someone leaves the company.
Give a shared mailbox as the point of contact. Then less changes.

The law does not require a fixed yearly check. It requires you to be quick when something changes.

3_1.headline: Plan what happens in an incident
3_1.teaser: Who decides, whom you call, how you reach each other.
missed: The law explicitly names secured voice, video and text communication and, where needed, secured emergency communication systems within the company (§ 30(2) no. 10 BSIG). A phone list on paper does not replace that; it is the fallback when everything else is down.
Decide who writes the report to {authority}. The first report, an early warning, is due at the latest 24 hours after you become aware of a significant incident (Art. 23(4)(a) NIS 2).
The plan only helps if it is at hand in an emergency. If it lives only on the server, it is gone with the server. Keep a copy where it can be found without IT, for example on paper or on a phone.

learn.title: When something happens
body: During an incident there is no time to work out who does what. So write it down beforehand: who decides, whom you call, and how you reach each other when email and the network are down.
A significant incident also has to be reported to {authority}, the first report within 24 hours. Your plan names who makes sure that happens; the next step, 3.3, shows how reporting works.

At the end of this step you have your incident response plan, written from your answers. For all staff, Germany's BSI publishes an IT emergency card to put up: it says what to do in an IT emergency and carries your IT emergency number.
learn.duty: The law requires your company to be able to handle security incidents.
learn.link: See the BSI's IT emergency card (in German)

lead.title: Your emergency contacts
lead.lead: One person leads in an emergency (a security incident). Everyone calls one number. You know how to reach each other when email and the network are down, and whom the person leading calls next.

plan.title: Your incident response plan
plan.lead: Written from your answers: who decides, whom you call, what to do first, how you report to {authority} and how you get back to normal. Read it, then add below what fits your company. An answer still missing shows as a line.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This plan sets out what happens at {company} when an IT security incident occurs or is suspected: who decides, whom we call, how we reach each other, how we report and how we get back to normal. It applies to all staff. A copy is kept where it can be found without IT, for example on paper.

sections.heading: If you notice something
sections.text: Anyone who notices or suspects an incident calls the IT emergency number {itEmergencyNumber} at once. If in doubt, call. On the phone, say who you are, which device or program is affected, what you saw, when it started and where the device is. Stop working on the affected device and do nothing further until you are told what to do. Write down what you saw.

sections.heading: Who leads
sections.text: {incidentLead} leads the response to an incident. This person decides whether an event is a mere disruption or a security incident and whether it has to be reported, and notes every decision with the time. They keep management informed. If they cannot be reached, management takes over.

sections.heading: Whom we call
sections.text: Depending on how serious the incident is, the lead calls: {incidentEscalationContacts}. A printed list with all phone numbers is kept with this plan, so we have the numbers without a computer or a digital address book. We keep it up to date.

sections.heading: How we reach each other when IT fails
sections.text: If email, the phone system or the network fail, we reach each other through: {secureCommsChannel}. Everyone on the list knows this channel and has set it up before it is needed.

sections.heading: First steps
sections.text: People's safety comes before everything else. Affected devices are taken off the network only on the lead's instruction. Before anyone examines or reinstalls a device, we secure logs, photos of the screen and notes. We write down everything that happens, with the time.

sections.heading: Reporting to the authority
sections.text: If an incident is significant, {company} reports it to the competent CSIRT or authority, through {reportingChannel}: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month of the notification (Art. 23(4) NIS 2). {incidentLead} makes sure the reports are made. The early warning says whether we suspect an unlawful or malicious act and whether the incident could affect other countries; everything else we know so far follows with the notification. If personal data is affected, we usually also notify the data protection authority, where feasible within 72 hours (Art. 33 GDPR).

sections.heading: Getting back to normal
sections.text: Affected systems go back into use only once the lead agrees: when the cause has been found and removed, restored from backups we know are clean. Afterwards we check that they work as before.

sections.heading: After the incident
sections.text: Once the incident is dealt with, the lead declares it over and records what happened. We discuss what went well and what did not, and change rules, measures and this plan where needed.

clauses.label: IT service provider
clauses.heading: IT service provider
clauses.text: Our IT service provider supports us in an incident. We have agreed with them how and when they can be reached, including outside business hours.

clauses.label: Outside business hours
clauses.heading: Outside business hours
clauses.text: The IT emergency number can also be reached outside business hours. Who answers it then is on the phone list.

clauses.label: IT emergency card
clauses.heading: IT emergency card
clauses.text: A copy of the BSI's IT emergency card (IT-Notfallkarte) with our number {itEmergencyNumber} is posted at every workplace.

clauses.label: Police
clauses.heading: Police
clauses.text: After an attack we consider reporting it to the police, through its cybercrime contact point for businesses where there is one.

clauses.label: Informing customers
clauses.heading: Informing customers
clauses.text: If an incident may affect our services to customers, management decides when and how we inform them.

clauses.label: Annual exercise
clauses.heading: Exercise
clauses.text: Once a year we walk through an incident using this plan and update the plan afterwards.

done.title: Your incident response plan is written
done.note: Make sure all staff know the emergency number, for example on the BSI's IT emergency card.

incidentLead.label: Who leads in an emergency (incident)
incidentLead.hint: The person who decides what to do and keeps management informed. In a small company this is often whoever looks after NIS 2.

itEmergencyNumber.label: Emergency number everyone calls
itEmergencyNumber.hint: Usually the mobile number of the person who leads. If an IT service provider takes these calls for you, their number. It is also the number on the BSI's IT emergency card.

secureCommsChannel.label: How you reach each other when email and the network are down (at least two ways)
secureCommsChannel.hint: Name at least two ways that do not depend on your own IT. Email, and a chat that runs on the same accounts as your email, can fail together with it.
suggestions: Messenger group on the company phones

incidentEscalationContacts.label: Whom the person leading calls next
incidentEscalationContacts.hint: Names and phone numbers, by how serious the incident is. Tap an answer, then add the name and number. No law asks for a second person; the plan already says management takes over if the person leading cannot be reached.

3_3.headline: Know how to report an incident
3_3.teaser: Three reports to {authority}, with fixed deadlines.
missed: The clock runs from when you learn of it, not from when everything is clear. Report early; the second report confirms or updates the first.
In Germany the BSI reads "becoming aware" as the moment someone in the company finds out about the incident during working hours (BSI, Meldepflicht info pack).

If it is a personal data breach, you usually also notify the data protection authority: without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the people affected (Art. 33 GDPR).

learn.title: Reporting an incident
body: If a security incident is significant, you report it to your national CSIRT or {authority}. It is significant if it can seriously disrupt your operations or cause you financial losses, or if it can cause considerable damage to others.
Your country sets the channel. In Germany it is the BSI portal, with the same access as for the registration.
learn.duty: You report significant incidents in three steps with fixed deadlines.

clock.title: The three deadlines
clock.lead: The clock runs from the moment your company learns of the incident. The third deadline starts with the second report.
clock.source: Art. 23(4) NIS 2. If {authority} asks for one, an interim report comes in between. If the incident is still going on after a month, send a progress report instead of the final report, and the final report within a month of dealing with it.

first_report.title: What the reporting form will ask
first_report.caption: You report in {authority}'s portal, never here. In Germany the BSI's form asks for these details in the early warning, one after the other. Answered here for a made-up case, so nothing on the form surprises you

rows.name: Classification
rows.detail: Significant incident; situation: orange, operations restricted

rows.name: Description
rows.detail: Files on the file server are encrypted and a ransom note was left. Accounting and order intake are down. Probably caused by an email attachment; duration still unknown.

rows.name: Times
rows.detail: Probably started around 6:30, detected at 7:40, this report as of 10:15

rows.name: Affected areas
rows.detail: Manufacturing, machinery; no critical facility

rows.name: Suspected attack
rows.detail: Yes, the ransom note points to a deliberate attack

rows.name: Other countries
rows.detail: Possible: customers in Austria will receive their deliveries late

rows.name: Measures
rows.detail: File server taken off the network, IT service provider on site, yesterday's backup checked

rows.name: Under control
rows.detail: No, the investigation is ongoing

rows.name: Reporting person
rows.detail: Anna Weber, head of IT, with phone and email for questions

first_report.note: The law asks for only two things in the early warning: whether the incident is suspected of being caused by unlawful or malicious acts, and whether it could have a cross-border impact (Art. 23(4)(a) NIS 2). The rest is what the reporting form asks for. Whatever you do not know yet, you add with the second report.

setup.title: Can you report today?
setup.lead: Check it now, not during an incident. You report to your country's CSIRT or competent authority; yours is below.
steps: Open the portal of {authority} below. In Germany that is the BSI portal.
Sign in with the access from your registration. In Germany that is the ELSTER organisation certificate file and its password.
Check that you can see where to report. In the BSI portal it is the red button "Sicherheitsvorfall melden" on the start page. Do not send anything.
Answer below: yes if the person who leads in an emergency, or their deputy, can do this.
setup.source: Art. 23(1) NIS 2. In Germany, § 32(1) BSIG: reports go to the reporting office the BSI runs together with the BBK, reached through the BSI portal (BSI, instructions for reporting in the BSI portal). A company that is not registered yet reports through an online form in the BSI's reporting and information portal (MIP).

bsiReportingRegistered.label: We can sign in to the portal and report
bsiReportingRegistered.hint: No, for example, if only one person has the login and is away, if the certificate file sits on the computer of someone who has left, or if nobody remembers its password. Sort that out first, then come back.

12_2.headline: Register with {authority}
missed: After registering, you report any change to these details within two weeks (Art. 3(4) NIS 2).

learn.title: Registering with {authority}
body: If NIS 2 applies to your company, it registers once with {authority}, the one in charge in your country. You tell it who you are and how to reach you.
Each member state runs its own registration, usually online. The next screen shows where yours is.
learn.duty: Registration is a duty of its own, with a deadline set by your country's law. In Germany it is three months after your company first counts as an important or essential entity.

where.title: Where you register
where.lead: You register in the member state where your company is established. Your country is at the top.
where.source: Art. 26(1) NIS 2: the member state of establishment is in charge. Providers of public electronic communications networks or services register where they provide their services. Providers of cloud computing, data centre and managed services, and similar digital providers, register where their main establishment is.

confirmation.title: Record the registration
confirmation.lead: Two details, so you know later which access was used and on which day. In Germany the access needs an ELSTER organisation certificate: its activation code comes by letter, a few days after you apply, to the address your tax office has. If the letter has not arrived yet, choose "Not possible yet".
confirmation.document: Your access to the portal of {authority}

mukAccountId.label: Account or reference at the portal
mukAccountId.hint: The ID of the account you registered with, or the reference number the portal gave you. In Germany it is the Benutzerkonto-ID of the ELSTER organisation certificate.

bsiRegistrationDate.label: Date of registration
bsiRegistrationDate.hint: The day the registration was submitted in the portal.

2_1.headline: Decide how you rate risks
2_1.teaser: We recommend a ready-made risk assessment method.
missed: Attacks are not the only thing that counts. The law requires an all-hazards approach (§ 30(2) BSIG). The EU directive explicitly requires protecting the physical environment of the systems too (Art. 21(2) NIS 2), for example against fire, water or a power cut.

learn.title: How you rate risks
body: Before you write down risks, decide how you rate them. Then everyone in the company rates them by the same rules.

nisd2.eu recommends a simple, ready-made risk assessment method. Every risk gets two ratings: how often can it happen, and how big would the damage be? Together they give one of four levels. The method comes from BSI Standard 200-3, published by Germany's Federal Office for Information Security.
learn.duty: The law requires concepts for risk analysis. It does not prescribe a particular method.

matrix.title: An example risk matrix
matrix.lead: Across: how often something happens. Down: how big the damage would be. Where the two meet is the level.
matrix.source: BSI Standard 200-3, Figure 3. It is given there as an example, to be adapted to the organisation's own needs.

reading.title: How to read the matrix
reading.caption: Six examples, from low to very high. Pick one and the matrix shows where it lands.
examples: A company phone gets lost, which happens once a year to once a month. It is encrypted and can be locked remotely, so the damage is negligible.
A server goes down once a year to once a month. The damage is limited and manageable.
A fire destroys the server room and all data in it. That happens at most every five years, but it would threaten the existence of the company.
Someone falls for a fake email, and invoices with a wrong bank account go out from the hijacked mailbox. That happens once a year to once a month, and the damage is considerable.
Ransomware encrypts every system and the backups too. That happens once every five years to once a year and would threaten the existence of the company.
The unmaintained inventory system goes down several times a month. Each time shipping stops for a day, and the damage is considerable.

adopt.title: Adopt the risk assessment method
adopt.lead: We give you the ready-made method from BSI Standard 200-3 as your template. One click makes it your company's risk assessment method, and from then on you rate every risk by it. This is how it appears in your records:

lines.label: Risk assessment method
lines.text: Risk analysis according to BSI Standard 200-3

lines.label: Levels
lines.text: Four for frequency, four for damage, four risk levels

lines.label: Matrix
lines.text: The assignment from Figure 3 of the standard

2_2.headline: Write down what your company has
2_2.teaser: A list of the processes, software and devices you work with.
missed: Software you rent from the cloud belongs on the list too, for example email or accounting.

learn.title: What your company works with
body: You can only protect what you know. So write down what your company works with: processes, information, software, devices, data carriers, rooms and networks. Germany's BSI works the same way and calls this step the structure analysis (Standard 200-2).
The list does not have to be perfect. When something new comes along, add it.
learn.duty: The law requires concepts for risk analysis and for managing your IT systems, products and processes. A list of what your company works with is the usual first step for both.

list.title: What your list can look like
list.caption: Short is fine. One line per thing:

rows.name: Payroll
rows.detail: done by the tax adviser

rows.name: Email
rows.detail: Microsoft 365, all staff

rows.name: Office PCs
rows.detail: twelve, at the main office

processes.title: What your company does every day
processes.lead: Tick what runs at your company. When in doubt, write it down rather than leave it out.

business_apps.title: Software for customers, staff and money
business_apps.lead: What you use to serve customers, pay wages and keep the books.

shared_apps.title: Software everyone uses
shared_apps.lead: Email, file storage, chat and anything only your industry has.

technology.title: Technology and rooms
technology.lead: Servers, devices, network and the places where people work.

which_software.title: Which software exactly, and from whom?
which_software.lead: Write down what you actually use, for example "DATEV Unternehmen online" instead of the kind "Accounting". Next to it goes who provides it: whoever sends you the invoice for it. Your bookkeeping, for example in DATEV, lists everyone you pay.

which_technology.title: Which technology exactly, and from whom?
which_technology.lead: The same for devices, network and rooms, for example the name of your internet provider for the internet connection. What you run yourself has no provider.

done.title: Your list is in place
done.note: When something new comes along, add it to the list at any time.

2_3.headline: Rate your risks
2_3.teaser: Place every piece of software, every device and every supplier on the matrix.
missed: Suppliers count too. The directive requires supply chain security, including the relationships with each direct supplier or service provider (Art. 21(2)(d) NIS 2), taking into account the vulnerabilities specific to each of them (Art. 21(3) NIS 2).
Rare does not mean small. In the BSI matrix, damage that threatens the existence of the organisation is never low, even if it could occur every 5 years at the most.

learn.title: How big is which risk?
body: Your list is in place: software, technology and suppliers. Now you rate each entry with the risk assessment method you set. How often does the worst realistic case happen, and how big would the damage be? The matrix turns that into one of four levels.
That shows you where protection is needed first. Individual threats, for example from the BSI's list of elementary threats, can be added afterwards in the risk register.
learn.duty: The law requires policies on risk analysis. How much protection is proportionate depends, among other things, expressly on the likelihood of incidents and their severity (Art. 21(1) NIS 2).

software.title: Rate your software
software.lead: Each program on your list has its own row. Think of its worst realistic case: it goes down, it is attacked or data is lost. Then tap the field in its matrix: further right, the more often it happens; further up, the bigger the damage.

technology.title: Rate your technology and rooms
technology.lead: The same for servers, devices, network and rooms. Think of fire, water and power cuts too.

suppliers.title: Rate your suppliers
suppliers.lead: Here the worst case is that the supplier fails or has a security incident of its own. The level then also shows in your supplier list.

map.title: Your risks at a glance
map.lead: Each number counts your entries in that field of the matrix. The further up and to the right, the sooner an entry needs protection. Below, all of them by name, highest level first.

2_4.headline: Write the security policy
2_4.teaser: A short policy that management approves.
missed: Everyone has to know the policy. Announce it to all staff and explain it to new staff before they get access to the systems; Germany's BSI asks for both (IT-Grundschutz ISMS.1.A3, Standard 200-2).

A policy goes out of date. Germany's BSI recommends reviewing it at least every two years (Standard 200-2). Digital providers covered by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 review it at least annually (Annex, point 1.1.2).

learn.title: Your information security policy
body: The information security policy is a short document of principles: what it covers, which objectives your company pursues, who is responsible and how it goes about security. The BSI, Germany's Federal Office for Information Security, calls it the visible commitment of management.

Our template covers what the BSI names as the minimum content. You add what applies to your company, management approves it, and all staff receive it. According to the BSI, more than ten pages are rarely needed.
learn.duty: The law requires policies on information system security (Art. 21(2)(a) NIS 2), and management bodies approve the risk-management measures and oversee their implementation (Art. 20(1) NIS 2). The policy is the document in which management puts that in writing.

leitlinie.title: Your policy
leitlinie.lead: The template covers what the BSI names as the minimum content of a policy, and your company's name is already in it. Read it, then add below what fits your company.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text: This policy applies to all of {company}: to all staff, all locations and all information, software, devices and services the company works with. It also applies where a service provider runs any of these for us.

sections.heading: Why information security matters to us
sections.text: Our work depends on information and on the IT that processes it. If they fail, are altered or reach the wrong hands, we cannot deliver our services and we harm our customers. Information security is therefore part of management's responsibilities.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: We protect the availability, confidentiality and integrity of our information and systems. Our services should keep running when something goes wrong, data of customers, staff and partners should be accessible only to those authorised, and our records should stay accurate and complete. These objectives serve the company's aim of delivering reliably and keeping its customers' trust.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.text: We work from the risks. We keep a list of our processes, software, devices and suppliers, assess the risks by a defined method and take measures that fit our size and the risks. In doing so we consider all hazards, including fire, water and power cuts.

sections.heading: Responsibility and organisation
sections.text: Management is responsible for information security. It approves the measures and oversees their implementation. It decides who coordinates information security day to day and provides the time, money and staff for it. All staff follow the rules that derive from this policy and report anything unusual immediately.

sections.heading: Enforcement and review
sections.text: Management enforces this policy and checks regularly whether the measures work. For this, the person who coordinates information security reports to management which measures are in place, where there were problems and what they propose. Management decides what changes, records the result and its decisions in writing, and makes sure gaps are closed. It reviews the policy itself regularly, after major changes in the company and after serious security incidents, and adapts it.

sections.heading: Announcement and entry into force
sections.text: The policy takes effect when management approves it. All staff receive it. New staff get to know it before they are given access to our systems.

clauses.label: Laws and contracts
clauses.heading: Laws and contracts
clauses.text: We comply with the laws and contracts that concern our information security, in particular the national law implementing the NIS 2 Directive, the General Data Protection Regulation and our agreements with customers. All staff are required to observe them.

clauses.label: Contact person
clauses.heading: Contact person
clauses.text: Questions about information security and reports of incidents go to the person who coordinates information security. Who that is can be found in the current overview of roles.

clauses.label: Training
clauses.heading: Training and awareness
clauses.text: All staff receive regular training in information security. Management itself takes part in training regularly.

clauses.label: Suppliers and service providers
clauses.heading: Suppliers and service providers
clauses.text: Anyone who works for us and has access to our systems or data also follows the rules of this policy. We agree this with our suppliers and service providers.

clauses.label: Reporting security incidents
clauses.heading: Reporting security incidents
clauses.text: Staff report security incidents and suspected incidents internally and immediately. The company reports significant incidents to the competent CSIRT or authority within the legal deadlines.

clauses.label: Consequences of violations
clauses.heading: Violations
clauses.text: Violations of this policy and of the rules that derive from it may have consequences under employment law.

clauses.label: Annual review
clauses.heading: Annual review
clauses.text: Management reviews this policy at least once a year.

clauses.label: Indicators
clauses.heading: Indicators
clauses.text: For the review we use a few figures, such as how many security updates are installed and how quickly we respond to incidents.

clauses.label: Independent check
clauses.heading: Independent check
clauses.text: At least once a year a qualified person who is not responsible for the measures checks whether they work.

done.title: Your policy is written
done.note: Once management has approved it, announce it to all staff, for example by email or on the intranet.

9_1.headline: Write the cryptography policy
9_1.teaser: Where you encrypt, and who keeps the keys.
missed: The recovery key of an encrypted disk does not belong on the same device. The IT-Grundschutz of Germany's BSI requires long-lived keys to be kept offline, outside the systems in use (CON.1.A2).
An encrypted backup only helps while the key exists. If the key is lost with the server, so is the backup. The IT-Grundschutz requires encrypted data to stay accessible over long periods (CON.1.A2).
Certificates expire. When your website's certificate has expired, browsers warn your visitors. The IT-Grundschutz requires time-limited certificates to be renewed in time (CON.1.A4).

learn.title: Where you encrypt, and who holds the keys
body: Encryption protects data where it can slip out of your hands: on a lost laptop, on its way across the internet, in a backup kept off site. Without the key, nobody can read it.

Two things record it: your list of accepted methods, and the cryptography policy, which says where you encrypt and how you handle keys and certificates, such as your website's, and prints the list. Which methods count as secure is set out in Technical Guideline TR-02102, which Germany's BSI updates every year.
learn.duty: The law requires policies and procedures for the use of cryptography and, where appropriate, encryption. It does not say which methods; the measures take the state of the art into account.

list.title: Your accepted methods
list.lead: The methods your company uses for encryption, signatures and secure connections, and the ones it no longer uses. Until you keep a list of your own, this is what Germany's BSI recommends in TR-02102; your policy on the next screen prints it.

status.deprecated: Only for what exists, not for anything new

list.change: Change single entries on the requirement page

konzept.title: Your cryptography policy
konzept.lead: The template has fixed sections on methods, keys and responsibility, and your company's name is already in it. Read it, then add below where you encrypt. Whoever looks after your IT can tell you what is already set up.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This policy sets out how {company} uses encryption and other cryptographic methods, so that unauthorised people can neither read information nor change it unnoticed. It applies to all devices, software and services the company works with, including those a service provider runs for us.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text:
We use only established methods and currently recommended key lengths with no known vulnerabilities. When we buy devices, software or services, we make sure they use such methods. Our list of methods:
{acceptedCrypto}

sections.heading: Keys and certificates
sections.text: We keep secret keys and recovery keys where unauthorised people cannot reach them, and apart from the devices they unlock. We renew certificates, such as our website's, before they expire. If a key has fallen into the wrong hands, or we suspect it has, we replace it. We securely delete keys we no longer need.

sections.heading: Responsibility
sections.text: Management decides who implements this policy and who manages keys and certificates. Where a service provider runs systems for us, we agree with them that they follow this policy. Everyone who sets up or looks after encrypted systems knows it.

sections.heading: Review
sections.text: We review this policy regularly. If a method we use becomes known to be insecure, we secure it or replace it.

clauses.label: TR-02102 as the benchmark
clauses.heading: Benchmark
clauses.text: Which methods and key lengths count as secure we take from Technical Guideline TR-02102 of Germany's BSI, in its current version.

clauses.label: Laptops
clauses.heading: Laptops
clauses.text: The disks of all laptops are encrypted.

clauses.label: Work phones and tablets
clauses.heading: Work phones and tablets
clauses.text: Work phones and tablets are protected by a screen lock, and their storage is encrypted.

clauses.label: USB sticks
clauses.heading: USB sticks and external drives
clauses.text: Anyone who takes company data along on a USB stick or an external drive encrypts it.

clauses.label: Backups
clauses.heading: Backups
clauses.text: Backups kept off site or with a service provider are encrypted. We keep the key separately, so that we can still read the backup after an outage.

clauses.label: Website and remote access
clauses.heading: Website and remote access
clauses.text: Our website and remote access to our systems can be reached only over encrypted connections.

clauses.label: Confidential email
clauses.heading: Confidential email
clauses.text: We send especially confidential content by email only when it is encrypted so that only the recipient can read it, for example with S/MIME or PGP.

clauses.label: Annual review
clauses.heading: Annual review
clauses.text: At least once a year we check whether the methods and key lengths we use are still secure enough.

clauses.label: Quantum-safe methods
clauses.heading: Quantum-safe methods
clauses.text: For data that must stay confidential for many years, we plan the move to quantum-safe methods following the BSI's recommendations.

done.title: Your cryptography policy is written
done.note: Give it to everyone who sets up your devices and services, including your IT service provider.

10_1.headline: Write the staff, access and asset policy
10_1.teaser: Who gets into what, and what happens when someone leaves.
missed: Accounts in cloud services that do not hang off the company login are easily forgotten when someone leaves. Germany's BSI counts a missing central overview among the important risks, because then not all accounts can be blocked at once in an emergency.

Your IT provider's remote maintenance access is an access like any other: only as far as the job needs it, and it ends with the job. The IT-Grundschutz of Germany's BSI requires outside staff to hand back their access when they leave (ORP.2.A4).

learn.title: Who gets into what
body: Access is created when someone starts. It becomes a risk when it stays after it is no longer needed: after a change of role, after someone leaves, after a contract ends. Germany's BSI counts exactly that among the important risks.

This policy covers, in one document, the three things the law names here: the security of your staff, who may access what, and how you manage your IT. For the IT part, your list of software, devices and suppliers is the basis.
learn.duty: The law requires human resources security, access control policies and asset management.

leaver.title: The last working day
leaver.caption: What happens to the access when someone leaves

good.value: On the last working day, IT blocks every account, including those in cloud services. Laptop, keys and badge come back.
good.note: The IT-Grundschutz asks for both: remove the user IDs, and collect documents, keys, devices and badges (ORP.4.A2, ORP.2.A2).

bad.value: The account stays open until someone remembers it.
bad.note: The BSI counts accounts of former staff that are not deleted among the important risks.

konzept.title: Your policy for staff, access and IT
konzept.lead: The template has fixed sections on joining, changing role and leaving, on outside staff, on access and on managing your IT, and your company's name is already in it. Read it, then add below what applies to you.

document.title: Staff, access and asset policy of {company}

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: This policy sets out how {company} makes sure that staff handle information securely, that only authorised people get into software and data, and that we know which systems and software we have.

sections.heading: New staff
sections.text: New staff are bound to confidentiality and learn the information security policy and the rules that apply to their work. Only then do they get access to our systems, and only the access their job needs.

sections.heading: Change of role and leaving
sections.text: When someone changes role, we adjust their access and remove what is no longer needed. When someone leaves the company, we block their access without delay, take back documents, devices, keys and badges, and remind them that confidentiality still applies.

sections.heading: Service providers and other outside staff
sections.text: Outside staff get only the access their job needs, and only for as long as it lasts. Before they see confidential information, we bind them to confidentiality in writing.

sections.heading: Access and rights
sections.text: Every user ID belongs to exactly one person. We grant rights only as far as the job needs them. Management decides who approves access and who sets it up.

sections.heading: Managing our IT
sections.text: We keep a list of our processes, software, devices and suppliers and keep it up to date. Anything new goes on the list before we use it. Devices and storage media we retire are securely wiped or destroyed, and taken off the list.

sections.heading: Review
sections.text: We review this policy regularly and after major changes in the company.

clauses.label: Reviewing rights
clauses.heading: Review of access rights
clauses.text: Once a year we check who may access which software and data, and remove what is no longer needed. Accounts with administrator rights are checked every quarter. We record the result.

clauses.label: Separate administrator accounts
clauses.heading: Administrator accounts
clauses.text: Administrator rights sit only on separate administrator accounts. For email and the internet, administrators also use an account without those rights.

clauses.label: Second factor for administrators
clauses.heading: Second factor for administrators
clauses.text: Accounts with administrator rights sign in only with a second factor, such as an app on the work phone or a security key.

clauses.label: Rights through roles
clauses.heading: Roles
clauses.text: We grant rights through roles, such as accounting or sales, and not to individual accounts.

clauses.label: Shared accounts
clauses.heading: Shared accounts
clauses.text: Accounts that several people use together exist only as a justified exception and with management's approval.

clauses.label: Unused accounts
clauses.heading: Unused accounts
clauses.text: Accounts that have not been used for a long time are blocked.

clauses.label: Passwords
clauses.heading: Passwords
clauses.text: Each password is used for one system only, kept secret, and changed as soon as there is a suspicion that it has become known.

clauses.label: Visitors
clauses.heading: Visitors
clauses.text: Visitors, tradespeople and other outsiders who are only briefly on site enter rooms with servers or network equipment only when accompanied.

clauses.label: Deputies
clauses.heading: Deputies
clauses.text: For important tasks a deputy is named who knows what to do.

done.title: Your policy is written
done.note: Use it whenever someone starts, changes role or leaves.

11_1.headline: Record where a second factor protects
11_1.teaser: For each program on your list: password alone, or with a second factor.
missed: Your IT provider's remote maintenance access is also access from outside. Grundschutz++ of Germany's BSI recommends a second factor that also resists phishing for everything reachable from outside (BER.5.8).
Administrator accounts first: Grundschutz++ recommends the second factor explicitly for access with far-reaching rights (BER.5.9).

learn.title: A password and something you hold
body: A password can be guessed, intercepted or found in someone else's data leak. A second factor is something you hold as well: an app on the work phone that shows a code or confirms the sign-in, or a security key. Anyone who only knows the password then cannot get in.

The law sets no particular assurance level, says Germany's BSI; you decide from your risk analysis. In this step you mark, for each program on your list, whether signing in already takes a second factor.
learn.duty: The law requires solutions where signing in takes more than a password (multi-factor authentication) or is checked continuously (continuous authentication).

where_first.title: Where first
where_first.caption: Which sign-ins need a second factor first

good.value: Email, remote access and administrator accounts with an app or a security key
good.note: Grundschutz++ recommends the second factor for everything reachable from outside and for access with far-reaching rights (BER.5.8, BER.5.9).

bad.value: Remote access from home with a password only
bad.note: Then a guessed or intercepted password is enough to get into your network.

good.value: Every user of the company's cloud account with an authenticator app
good.note: One account usually opens email, files and chat at once, so one stolen password would open all three.

bad.value: A second factor for management only
bad.note: A phishing email reaches every inbox, and attackers use whichever account is easiest.

good.value: Administrator accounts with a security key
good.note: A security key checks which website it signs in to, so a fake sign-in page cannot use it.

bad.value: Administrator accounts with codes by SMS
bad.note: A text message can be redirected to another SIM card. For accounts with full rights, choose an app or a key.

logins.title: Where a second factor protects
logins.lead: For each program and access on your list, mark how people sign in, and where a second factor is on, which one: it can differ from program to program. Each row starts at "Password only", the safe assumption; change it where you know better, or mark "Not known yet". Where several are reached through one company account, for example with Microsoft, they share the same answer. Whoever looks after your IT can tell you what you do not know.

done.title: Your sign-ins are recorded
done.note: Where only a password is marked, decide from the risk whether to switch on a second factor. Start with what is reachable from outside.

11_2.headline: Record secured communication
11_2.teaser: What you use for calls, meetings and messages.
missed: Encrypted transfer protects the way, not the message on the server. For especially confidential content Germany's BSI advises encryption that only sender and recipient can read as well, for example S/MIME or PGP for email.

learn.title: Phone, video, chat
body: For calls, meetings and messages you use programs and services. Secured here means: the transfer is encrypted, and only authorised people get in. The BSI names the TLS protocol as the standard for securing the transfer.
How you reach each other when your own IT fails is already in your incident response plan. In this step you record what you use to talk and write day to day.
learn.duty: The law requires secured voice, video and text communication within the company and, where appropriate, secured emergency communication.

answer.title: An answer that holds
answer.caption: How to record what you communicate with

good.value: Email and chat in Microsoft 365, meetings in Teams, phone calls over the provider's cloud phone system, all transferred encrypted
good.note: Names every tool and says how it is secured.

bad.note: Says nothing about what you use, and cannot be checked.

tools.title: Your tools
tools.lead: What you use for calls, meetings and messages, and how it is secured. The law names voice, video and text together as one measure, so one answer covers all three. Tap the programs from your list that you use for this, then say how they are secured.

done.title: Your communication is recorded
done.note: When a new tool comes in, add it to this answer.

secureCommsTools.label: Tools for phone, video and chat
secureCommsTools.hint: For example: Microsoft Teams for meetings and chat, phone calls over the provider's cloud phone system, all transferred encrypted.
suggestions: Sign-in only with a company account
Guests join meetings only when let in

6_3.headline: Write the rules for buying, updates and vulnerabilities
6_3.teaser: What you check when buying, how updates arrive and who closes gaps.
missed: Software that no longer gets security updates stays vulnerable, even while it still runs. Check when buying how long the maker supplies updates.
Remote maintenance access that stays open all the time is a way in. Germany's BSI names switching it off in its NIS 2 information package on security measures.

learn.title: Buy, update, close gaps
body: A vulnerability is a property of software or a device that an outsider can exploit to get in or to disrupt it. That is how the law describes it. Examples: software that no longer gets updates, an update left waiting, a default password never changed.

The rules in this step set out what you check when buying, how updates are installed, how you handle vulnerabilities and where people can report one to you. Where an IT provider looks after your systems, the rules tell them what you expect.
learn.duty: The law requires security when you acquire, develop and maintain your IT, including handling and disclosing vulnerabilities.

good.value: Security updates install automatically, and the IT provider checks every month that everything is up to date.
good.note: Grundschutz++ of Germany's BSI recommends installing security updates automatically (KONF.8.1.1).

bad.note: Until then a known gap stays open that an attacker can exploit.

sources.title: Where vulnerabilities become known
sources.lead: You do not have to hunt for gaps yourself. New vulnerabilities are announced publicly, and your list of software from step 2.2 tells you which announcements concern you. These are the places to watch:

items.name: Makers' security notices
items.detail: the companies whose software and devices you use publish them on their website, and many send them by email if you sign up

items.name: The BSI's warning and information service
items.detail: CERT-Bund, part of Germany's BSI, publishes new vulnerabilities in widely used products at wid.cert-bund.de; you can subscribe by email free of charge

items.name: The European vulnerability database
items.detail: ENISA, the EU's cybersecurity agency, lists published vulnerabilities at euvd.enisa.europa.eu

items.name: Your IT provider
items.detail: whoever looks after your systems usually follows these sources already; agree in writing that they tell you when you are affected

sources.source: In its NIS 2 information package on security measures, Germany's BSI recommends checking systems regularly for known gaps and handling vulnerabilities by risk. The warning service: bsi.bund.de, Warning and Information Service (WID).

report.title: Where people report a vulnerability to you
report.lead: If someone finds a gap in your systems, for example on your website, they need an address for it. Germany's BSI recommends naming it publicly. Where your company has a contact email, the common answers below use its domain. If you have none yet, leave the field empty: your rules then get a line to fill in.
report.document: Your rules for buying, updates and vulnerabilities

rules.title: Your rules for buying, updates and vulnerabilities
rules.lead: The template has fixed sections on buying, updates, vulnerabilities and reports, and your company's name is already in it. Read it, then add below what applies to you.

document.title: Rules for buying, maintaining and securing the IT of {company}

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text: These rules apply to all software, devices, cloud services and networks {company} works with, including those a service provider runs for us.

sections.heading: When buying
sections.text: Before we buy software, a device or a cloud service, we check whether the provider supplies security updates and for how long. Where we can, we buy nothing with known, exploitable vulnerabilities and nothing whose support ends soon. At set-up we change default passwords.

sections.heading: Updates
sections.text: We install security updates as soon as they are available, automatically where possible. If an update cannot be installed, we record why and what we do instead.

sections.heading: Finding and fixing vulnerabilities
sections.text: We follow the security notices of the makers of our software and devices, the warnings of our national CSIRT and our IT provider's notices. If a vulnerability affects us, the person who coordinates information security decides with the IT provider what to do, serious vulnerabilities first. We record what we found and what we did.

sections.heading: Reporting vulnerabilities
sections.text: We take reports of vulnerabilities in our systems at {vulnerabilityDisclosureUrl}. If we find a vulnerability in a product we use, we report it to the maker. If the maker does not respond, we can report it to our national CSIRT.

sections.heading: Review
sections.text: We review these rules regularly and after major changes to our IT.

clauses.label: Only what is needed
clauses.heading: Set-up
clauses.text: We set up devices and software with only the functions we need. Services and accounts we do not need are switched off.

clauses.label: Remote maintenance
clauses.heading: Remote maintenance
clauses.text: Remote maintenance access is open only while maintenance is being done.

clauses.label: Providers' duties
clauses.heading: Providers' duties
clauses.text: We agree with our IT providers that they fix vulnerabilities affecting us without delay.

clauses.label: Regular checks
clauses.heading: Regular checks
clauses.text: We have our systems checked regularly for known vulnerabilities.

clauses.label: Major changes
clauses.heading: Major changes
clauses.text: We plan major changes to important systems beforehand, record them and keep a way back in case something goes wrong.

clauses.label: Our own software
clauses.heading: Our own software
clauses.text: If we develop software ourselves or have it developed, we set the security requirements beforehand and have it checked before it goes into use.

clauses.label: security.txt
clauses.heading: Reporting address on the website
clauses.text: Our website has a security.txt file under RFC 9116 that says where to report vulnerabilities.

done.title: Your rules are written
done.note: Give them to everyone who sets up and maintains your IT, including your IT provider.

vulnerabilityDisclosureUrl.label: Address for vulnerability reports
vulnerabilityDisclosureUrl.hint: An email address, for example security@ at your domain, or a web page. Germany's BSI recommends a security.txt file on your website for this (RFC 9116).

4_2.headline: Write the business continuity plan
4_2.teaser: How you keep working when something fails, and who decides then.
missed: Emergency operation does not mean everything runs as usual. For a start, Germany's BSI names fallback processes such as taking orders by hand and keeping records on paper (its guide to business continuity for small companies).
The plan only helps if it is at hand in an emergency. If it lives only on the server, it is gone with the server. Keep printed copies, one of them outside the building.

learn.title: When operations stop
body: The incident response plan says who calls whom and who decides during an attack. This plan goes further: it covers anything that interrupts important work, including fire, water, power cuts or the failure of an important provider. It says how you keep working, who restores the systems and who leads the crisis.

For a start, Germany's BSI recommends that smaller companies have a plan that keeps operations going at a minimum level: fallback processes, fallback places, and informing staff, suppliers and customers. Our template covers these points.
learn.duty: The law requires business continuity, such as backup management and disaster recovery, and crisis management.

good.value: We take orders by phone and on paper forms until the order system runs again.
good.note: A fallback process of the kind the BSI names for a start: orders by hand, records on paper.

bad.value: We wait until the IT works again.
bad.note: Until then no orders come in, and nobody knows how long that takes.

keep.title: What must keep running
keep.lead: These are the processes on your list. Ask of each one: if IT were gone for a whole day, could we simply wait, or would customers, safety or a deadline suffer? Tick the ones that cannot wait, and say in one sentence how they continue. Both then appear in your plan.
keep.example: for example: orders by phone and on paper forms

plan.title: Your business continuity plan
plan.lead: The template has fixed sections on leadership, emergency operation, recovery and informing people. Your company's name, the person who leads in an emergency (from step 3.1), the processes that must keep running and the order from your risk assessment are already in it. Read it, then add below what applies to you.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This plan sets out how {company} keeps working when an event interrupts important work: a cyber attack, an IT or internet outage, fire, water, a power cut or the failure of an important provider. It complements the incident response plan, which governs alerting and the first steps.

sections.heading: When this plan applies
sections.text: This plan applies when an event interrupts important work for longer than normal troubleshooting takes, or threatens to. In doubt, {emergencyLead} decides.

sections.heading: Leadership
sections.text: {emergencyLead}, who also leads under the incident response plan, leads the response, brings in the people needed, decides, and records each decision with the time. Decisions about money, customers and staff are taken together with management. If {emergencyLead} cannot be reached, management takes over.

sections.heading: Alerting and contacts
sections.text: Whom we call and how we reach each other when the IT fails is set out in the incident response plan, with the phone list on paper.

sections.heading: Emergency operation
sections.text: These processes must keep running, even without IT, and this is how they continue: {criticalProcesses}

sections.heading: Recovery
sections.text: Our IT provider or our own IT restores the systems from the backups. A system goes back into use only once it has been checked. The order follows the damage in our risk assessment, the largest first: {recoveryOrder}. In an emergency the lead can decide otherwise.

sections.heading: Informing people
sections.text: {emergencyLead} or someone they name informs staff, suppliers and customers. Reports to the competent CSIRT or authority follow the incident response plan.

sections.heading: Back to normal operation
sections.text: {emergencyLead} declares the emergency over. We record what happened and adapt this plan.

clauses.label: Recovery targets
clauses.heading: Recovery targets
clauses.text: For our most important systems we set how long they may be down at most and how much data may be lost at most. The figures are recorded with the systems on our list.

clauses.label: Yearly exercise
clauses.heading: Exercise
clauses.text: Once a year we walk through an outage around the table and check that we can reach everyone involved.

clauses.label: Fallback workplace
clauses.heading: Fallback workplace
clauses.text: If the office cannot be used, we keep working remotely or at a fallback location.

clauses.label: Power cut
clauses.heading: Power cut
clauses.text: For a power cut it is set which devices must keep running and who decides about emergency power.

clauses.label: Providers in an emergency
clauses.heading: Providers in an emergency
clauses.text: We have agreed with our important providers how we reach them in an emergency and what they then do for us.

clauses.label: Printed copy
clauses.heading: Printed copy
clauses.text: A printed copy of this plan is kept outside the building.

done.title: Your business continuity plan is written
done.note: Keep a copy that works without IT next to the incident response plan, for example on paper.

4_4.headline: Record your backups
4_4.teaser: How often you back up, and when a restore last worked.
missed: A backup with the same provider that holds the original data does not count as separate storage for Germany's BSI, cloud services included (Grundschutz++ NOT.4.10).
An attacker can encrypt a backup on the same network along with everything else. The BSI therefore recommends a copy kept separate from the network (Grundschutz++ NOT.4.14).

learn.title: A backup you can restore
body: A backup is a copy of your data that you bring back after an outage, an attack or a mistake. It only helps if a copy survives the incident and can really be restored.
In this step you record, for each backup system on your list, how often it backs up and when a restore from it last worked. Where the copies are kept stays on the requirement page.
learn.duty: The law names backup management and disaster recovery explicitly as part of business continuity.

copy.title: Where the copy is kept
copy.caption: A copy that survives an attack

good.value: One copy is kept off the network, for example on a disk in a cupboard or in storage that nobody can delete or change.
good.note: Grundschutz++ recommends keeping backups separate from the original data and one copy off the network (NOT.4.10, NOT.4.14).

bad.value: The backup sits on a drive in the same network as the server.
bad.note: If an attacker encrypts the server, the backup is encrypted along with it.

ask.title: What to ask first
ask.lead: Ask whoever looks after your IT, before you answer on the next screen:

items.name: Which backup systems
items.detail: what makes your backups, for example backup software, a NAS or a cloud backup service; each one is a line on the next screen

items.name: How often each one backs up
items.detail: continuously, hourly, daily or weekly, for the systems it backs up: servers, file storage, databases

items.name: The last restore from each
items.detail: when data last came back from it, and whether it was complete and readable; one sample is enough for the BSI

items.name: Your cloud and software providers, separately
items.detail: they back up their own systems; ask each one what they keep for you and how you would get your data back. Their answers do not go on the next screen

ask.source: Germany's BSI, emergency management checklist: make backups regularly and test regularly that they can be restored. Checking by samples: Grundschutz++ NOT.4.16.1. The law names backup management, not figures per system (§ 30(2) no. 3 BSIG).

systems.title: Your backup systems
systems.lead: Each backup system on your list, with what you were told. A backup that was never restored is not shown to work: the law asks for effective measures (§ 30(1) BSIG). That is our reading, not the wording of the law.
systems.lastRestore: Last restore from it that worked
systems.lastRestoreHint: The day data last came back from it complete, as a test or for real. If none has worked yet, leave it empty and plan one.
systems.empty: No backup system is on your list yet.
systems.add: Add a backup system to your list

done.title: Your backups are recorded
done.note: Germany's BSI advises testing restores regularly. Enter the new date after each test.

8_2.headline: Record your staff training
8_2.teaser: Who was briefed on what, and when.
missed: New staff need the briefing too. Germany's BSI considers it sensible to train people when they start and to inform everyone about what is new once a year.
Without a record, a training cannot be shown later. The BSI calls documenting the measures a necessary condition for meeting the requirement of the German act.

learn.title: What your staff should know
body: A phishing email, a call from a supposed IT support desk, an unknown USB stick: attacks like these are aimed at your staff. Whoever recognises them reports them instead of clicking.

Germany's BSI considers it sensible to train new staff when they start and to inform everyone about what is new once a year. Explaining your security policy and putting up a poster such as an IT emergency card count too; the BSI names conveying clear security rules and posters explicitly. What matters is that you record who took part and when.
learn.duty: The law requires basic cyber hygiene practices and cybersecurity training. It does not say how often, in what form or with which provider.
learn.link: The BSI's page on training (in German)

record.title: What records can look like
record.caption: One line per training or briefing:

rows.name: Spotting phishing, all staff
rows.detail: team meeting, 14 January 2026, list of who was there

rows.name: First-day briefing, new colleague in sales
rows.detail: first working day, 2 March 2026, security policy explained and handed over

rows.name: Online course on information security, administration
rows.detail: completed by 30 April 2026, export from the course

record.note: The law prescribes no format. Record what it covered, who took part and when.

trainings.title: Your trainings and briefings
trainings.lead: Enter what has already taken place, one line per session. Attach a list of who took part or an export, or link the record at the provider, for example an online course's completion report. That works for many staff at once too.

done.title: Your training is recorded
done.note: Enter future trainings on the Training page, including the briefing of new staff.

12_4.headline: Detect attacks and prove it to the BSI
12_4.teaser: Operators of critical facilities only: attack detection and the evidence every three years.
missed: If your company runs energy supply networks or energy installations and is subject to §§ 5c to 5e of the German Energy Industry Act (EnWG) for them, §§ 31 and 39 BSIG do not apply to those installations. They do apply to any other critical facility you run alongside (§ 28(5) BSIG).
If you were already an operator of critical infrastructure under the old BSI Act, the BSI sets the date at the earliest three years after your last evidence under the old law (§ 39(3) BSIG).

learn.title: Detect attacks automatically
body: Your company profile gives the entity type “KRITIS Operator”. That is why you see this step. Other companies do not have it.

For the IT your critical facility depends on, you run systems that detect attacks. They collect and evaluate data from operations continuously and automatically, so they spot threats and provide responses to disruptions.
The effort should stand in reasonable proportion to what an outage of the facility would cause.
learn.duty: Operators of critical facilities run attack detection systems for the IT that is essential to the operation of their facility.

detection.title: Which system detects attacks?
detection.lead: Name the system and which systems of the facility it watches. If none runs yet, choose “Not possible yet”.
detection.document: Attack detection of the critical facility

evidence.title: Every three years: evidence to the BSI
evidence.lead: Through a security audit, a test or a certification you prove to the BSI that your measures are in place, attack detection included. The BSI gets:

items.name: The result
items.detail: of the audit, test or certification

items.name: The deficiencies found
items.detail: every security deficiency the check uncovered

items.name: On request: the documents
items.detail: the check was based on

items.name: On request: a remediation plan
items.detail: and afterwards proof that the deficiencies are fixed

evidence.source: § 39(1) BSIG: at a date the BSI sets, at the earliest three years after your company first counts as an operator of a critical facility, then every three years.

last.title: When did the last evidence go to the BSI?
last.lead: The day your company last sent the BSI evidence, including evidence under the old law. If there has been none yet, leave the field empty and go on.

attackDetectionSystem.label: Attack detection system
attackDetectionSystem.hint: What it is, who runs it and which systems of the facility it watches. For example: our provider's SIEM, watching the control system network and the remote access points.
suggestions: Monitoring of the control system network

lastKritisEvidenceDate.label: Last evidence sent to the BSI
lastKritisEvidenceDate.hint: The date is on the cover letter of the evidence. Whoever sent it can tell you.

7_3.headline: Record the management review
7_3.teaser: Management checks whether the measures work and approves your documents.
missed: Management can only oversee what it knows. Germany's BSI advises reports to management that cover above all problems, successes and opportunities for improvement (IT-Grundschutz ISMS.1.A12).
Decisions without an owner and a date stay undone. For every task, record who does it by when.

learn.title: What management sees and decides
body: Sit down, look at where things stand, decide: that is the management review. The person who coordinates information security reports what is in place, where things are stuck and what they propose. Management decides what happens next and records it.
In this step you enter the review and approve the documents the walkthrough wrote, which are saved as drafts so far. The law does not say how often or in what form.
learn.duty: The law requires management bodies to approve the measures and oversee their implementation, and requires procedures to assess whether the measures are effective.

inputs.title: What goes on the table

items.name: What is in place
items.detail: the finished steps of this walkthrough and what is still open

items.name: Problems
items.detail: incidents, outages and anything that did not work

items.name: Risks
items.detail: your rated risks, highest first; they are on the next step

items.name: Proposals
items.detail: what the person who coordinates information security would change

inputs.source: Under IT-Grundschutz ISMS.1.A12 of Germany's BSI, reports to management cover in particular problems, successes and opportunities for improvement.

risks.title: Your risks for management
risks.lead: This is where your software, technology and suppliers stand today. The further up and to the right, the sooner an entry needs protection. Management decides where to act first.

record.title: What an entry can look like
record.caption: A management review, made up:

rows.name: Date and participants
rows.detail: 12 February 2026; management, information security coordinator, IT provider

rows.name: Looked at
rows.detail: walkthrough status, two incidents, the five highest risks

rows.name: Decided
rows.detail: policies approved; second factor for remote access

rows.name: To do
rows.detail: test a restore, IT provider, by the end of March; phishing briefing, coordinator, in April

record.note: The law prescribes neither a meeting nor minutes. Record the date, who took part, the decisions and the tasks.

review.title: Your management review
review.lead: Enter the review: when, who, what was decided and what has to be done.

approve.title: Management approves the documents
approve.lead: These are the documents this walkthrough wrote. Management reads each one and approves it here, signed in with its own account. Nothing is printed or scanned.

ongoing.title: From now on, in your hands
ongoing.lead: The approval records what your company does. From now on it is up to you to do it. These duties stay once the walkthrough is finished.

items.name: A significant incident
items.detail: An early warning to the BSI within 24 hours of becoming aware, the notification after 72 hours and the final report one month after the notification at the latest.

items.name: A registration detail changes
items.detail: Update it in the BSI's portal within two weeks of becoming aware. For example a new contact person or new public IP addresses.

items.name: The BSI orders you to inform your customers
items.detail: Inform the recipients of your services without undue delay.

items.name: A new program or a new service provider
items.detail: Add it to the list and assess its risk, as your security policy sets out under “Approach”.

items.name: The management review
items.detail: Repeat it so management oversees the implementation. The law sets no interval; if your security policy has the yearly review, a year applies.

items.name: Management training
items.detail: Every member, at least every three years, as the explanatory memorandum reads “regularly”.

items.name: Staff training
items.detail: The BSI considers it useful to train new staff when they start and to brief everyone on changes once a year.

items.name: Implement and oversee the measures
items.detail: Do what the documents set out: keep the second factor on, install security updates, test the restore.

items.name: Close the open points
items.detail: Act without undue delay on what the approval showed as still open.

done.title: Your management review is recorded
done.note: The approved documents apply from the day management approved them and are listed under your policies.
